summary: Extends the RSVP ASSOCIATION object, which in GMPLS associates recovery LSPs with the LSPs they protect. It defines how the object can be used more broadly to associate RSVP state. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6780 widens the RSVP ASSOCIATION object, which ties related pieces of RSVP state together. The object was built for GMPLS recovery, where a backup path is tied to the path it protects. This document lets it be used for any RSVP session, in both Path and Resv messages, and adds a larger form of the object so a node can name more associations and identify them globally.

questions: what is the rsvp association object
what is the extended association object
subtitle: Widening the RSVP ASSOCIATION object beyond GMPLS recovery, with larger identifiers for MPLS-TP.

tldr.problem: The RSVP ASSOCIATION object was defined to tie a recovery LSP to the LSP it protects. Its Association ID field is only 16 bits, so one node can name at most 65536 associations, and its rules only covered GMPLS recovery.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6780 generalizes the Association ID definition, gives rules for matching ASSOCIATION objects across RSVP sessions in both Path and Resv messages, and defines IPv4 and IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION objects that add a global source identifier and a variable-length extension field.
tldr.outcome: RSVP reservations in unrelated sessions can now be associated, so they can share bandwidth and other resources. The document updates RFC 2205, RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 4872 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6780 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2012. It updates RFC 2205, RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 4872, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
End-to-end and segment recovery for GMPLS-controlled Label Switched Paths are defined in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. Both use the ASSOCIATION object to tie recovery LSPs to the LSP they protect. RFC 6689 describes how such associations are identified.

This document expands the ASSOCIATION object to non-GMPLS and non-recovery contexts. The expanded usage applies to GMPLS LSPs, MPLS LSPs and non-LSP RSVP sessions alike. It also reviews how associations should be made when the object travels in a Path message, and defines usage with Resv messages.

Three non-LSP uses are given. With voice call-waiting, a bidirectional call between endpoints A and B is signalled as two separate unidirectional RSVP reservations, for A to B and B to A. If A wants to put the A-B call on hold and join a separate A-C call, it is useful for the network resources on common links to be shared. The B to A and C to A subflows can already share resources through the existing RSVP sharing mechanisms, but only if they use the same destination IP addresses and ports. Because the RSVP reservations for the subflows A to B and A to C must have different IP addresses in the SESSION objects, a new mechanism is needed to associate the subflows and let them share resources.

With a voice shared line, a single number rings several endpoints, which may be geographically diverse, such as phone lines to a manager's desk and to an assistant. A VoIP system that models these calls as multiple point-to-point unicast pre-ring reservations would over-count bandwidth on shared links, because RSVP unicast reservations to different endpoints cannot share bandwidth. A new mechanism lets separate unicast reservations be associated and share resources.

With symmetric NAT, RSVP already allows resources to be shared between multiple flows addressed to the same destination D, even from different senders S1 and S2. But if D is behind a NAT operating in symmetric mode, the destination port of the flows S1 to D and S2 to D may differ outside the NAT. The SESSION objects for the two flows then have different destination ports, so RSVP sharing does not apply. This document defines a mechanism to associate these flows.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP reservations normally cannot share bandwidth unless they have the same destination address and port. That blocks three everyday cases: a call on hold next to a new call, one number ringing several phones, and two senders reaching a host behind a NAT that changes the port. The ASSOCIATION object gives a way to say these separate reservations really belong together.

sections.title: Generalized Association ID Field
sections.content:
The Association ID field is carried in the IPv4 and IPv6 ASSOCIATION objects defined in RFC 4872. That document describes it as a value assigned by the LSP head-end which, combined with the Association Type and Association Source, uniquely identifies an association.

This document allows ASSOCIATION objects to be originated by nodes other than the LSP head-end, so the field is redefined as a value assigned by the node that originated the association, which when combined with the other fields carried in the object uniquely identifies an association.

The RFC states that this change in definition does not affect the procedures or mechanisms defined in RFC 4872 or RFC 4873, and does not affect existing implementations of either document. When the procedures in this document are used, association is identified by exact ASSOCIATION object matching. Some of the other matching mechanisms in RFC 4872, such as matching based on Session IDs, are not generalized. The document allows for, but does not specify, association type-specific processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The Association ID used to be defined as a number chosen by the head end of a path. The new wording is simpler: it is a number chosen by whichever node started the association, and together with the other fields in the object it names one association uniquely. Existing deployments are not affected.

sections.title: Upstream-Initiated Association in Path Messages
sections.content:
Upstream-initiated association is represented by ASSOCIATION objects carried in Path messages, and can be used to associate RSVP Path state across MPLS tunnels and RSVP sessions. An MPLS tunnel is represented by an RSVP SESSION object, and multiple LSPs may be represented within a single tunnel. Cross-LSP association based on Path state is defined in RFC 4872; this section extends that definition with generic association rules and non-LSP uses, and does not modify the processing required to support RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. The use of an ASSOCIATION object within a single session is not precluded.

In a Path message, the ASSOCIATION object may appear after the LABEL_REQUEST and optional SESSION_ATTRIBUTE in the MPLS and GMPLS case, and after the TIME_VALUES in the non-LSP case. In general the relative ordering of ASSOCIATION objects with respect to each other, and to other objects, is not significant, although transit nodes should preserve the relative ordering of ASSOCIATION objects of the same type.

A node sending a Path message chooses when to include an ASSOCIATION object. To indicate an association between multiple sessions, an appropriate ASSOCIATION object must be included in the outgoing Path messages of each associated session. In the absence of type-specific rules for identifying the association, the included ASSOCIATION object must be identical.

When creating an ASSOCIATION object, the originator must format it as defined in Section 16.1 of RFC 4872, set the Association Type field to the type of association being identified, set the Association ID field to a value that uniquely identifies the specific association within the context of the Association Source field, and set the Association Source field to a unique address assigned to the node originating the association.

A downstream node identifies an upstream-initiated association by checks. On receiving a Path message it must check each ASSOCIATION object for an Association Type value it supports. For each supported type it must then check whether the object matches an ASSOCIATION object received in any other Path message, by examining the Path state of all other sessions and comparing the fields of the newly received ASSOCIATION object with the fields of the ASSOCIATION objects in that state. An association exists when the same values are carried in all fields of the objects being compared. Because more than one association may exist, the matching must continue after a match is found and must be performed against all local Path state, and it is possible that no match is found at all.

Unless there are type-specific processing rules, downstream nodes must forward all ASSOCIATION objects received in a Path message in any corresponding outgoing Path messages without modification. This also applies to unknown Association Type values.
sections.plainLanguage: An upstream node that wants two sessions treated as related puts the same ASSOCIATION object in the Path message of each. Every node downstream compares the object it receives with the objects it holds for other sessions. Two objects that match in every field mean the sessions are associated. The objects are passed on unchanged, even when the node does not understand the association type.

sections.title: Downstream-Initiated Association in Resv Messages
sections.content:
Downstream-initiated association is represented by ASSOCIATION objects carried in Resv messages, and can be used to associate RSVP Resv state across MPLS tunnels and RSVP sessions. Cross-LSP association based on Path state is defined in RFC 4872; this section defines cross-session association based on Resv state. It places no additional requirements on implementations supporting RFC 4872 and RFC 4873, and it does not preclude the use of an ASSOCIATION object in a single session.

In a Resv message the ASSOCIATION object may appear after the optional RESV_CONFIRM and SCOPE objects and before the optional POLICY_DATA objects, with the STYLE and flow descriptor list following. The relative ordering of ASSOCIATION objects with respect to each other, and to other objects, is not currently significant, although transit nodes should preserve the relative ordering of ASSOCIATION objects of the same type.

A node that wishes to allow upstream nodes to associate Resv state across RSVP sessions must include an ASSOCIATION object in the outgoing Resv messages of the sessions to be associated, and the included objects must be identical in the absence of type-specific rules. The originator must format the object as in Section 16.1 of RFC 4872, set the Association Type to the type of association being identified, set the Association ID to a value that uniquely identifies the association within the context of the Association Source field, and set the Association Source to a unique address assigned to the originating node.

An upstream node identifies a downstream-initiated association by the same kind of checks applied to Path state: it must check each ASSOCIATION object in a received Resv message for a supported Association Type, then compare the object against the ASSOCIATION objects in the Resv state of all other sessions, with an association deemed to exist when the same values are carried in all fields of the objects being compared. Matching must continue after a match is found and must be performed against all local Resv state, and it is possible that no match is found. Unless type-specific processing rules exist, upstream nodes must forward all ASSOCIATION objects received in a Resv message in any corresponding outgoing Resv messages without modification, including for unknown Association Type values.

Association is always done by matching Path state to Path state, or Resv state to Resv state, never Path state to Resv state.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea works in the other direction. A node near the destination can put an ASSOCIATION object in the Resv messages of two sessions, and the nodes upstream compare it with the Resv state they hold. Path state and Resv state are never matched to each other.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION Objects
sections.content:
RFC 4872 defines the IPv4 and IPv6 ASSOCIATION objects, each with an Association Source field and a 16-bit Association ID field. Because the Association ID field is 16 bits wide, an association source can allocate up to 65536 different associations and no more. There are scenarios where this number is insufficient, for example where the association is best identified by a fairly centralised entity and is therefore involved in a large number of associations.

MPLS-TP LSPs present a case the existing objects cannot support. Per RFC 6370, MPLS-TP LSPs can be identified by an operator-unique global identifier, and the Global_ID defined there is based on RFC 5003 and includes the operator's Autonomous System Number.

Two new objects are defined to fix this. The IPv4 Extended ASSOCIATION object has class number 199 with C-Type 3, and the IPv6 Extended ASSOCIATION object has class number 199 with C-Type 4. Both add a 4-byte Global Association Source field, which holds a unique global identifier or the special value zero; when it is non-zero and not overridden by local policy, the Global_ID as defined in RFC 6370 must be used, and the special value zero means no global identifier is present, which should be limited to entities inside a single operator. If the value is derived from a 2-octet ASN, the two high-order octets of the field must be set to zero.

Both objects also add an Extended Association ID field of variable length, 4-byte aligned. It carries additional information to support unique identification, its length and contents are scoped by the Association Source, a length of zero means the field is omitted, and the object Length field is set from it. When the Extended Association ID is omitted, the object Length field must be set to 16 for the IPv4 object and 28 for the IPv6 object. When it is present, the Length field must indicate the extra bytes carried, including pad bytes. Per RFC 2205, the Length field is the total object length in bytes, is always a multiple of 4, and is at least 4.

Processing of an Extended ASSOCIATION object must be identical to processing of the ordinary object, except for these changes. The originator sets the Global Association Source field to the global identifier when ASN-based global identification is wanted, and to zero when it is not. The Extended Association ID may be included based on local policy, and must be included when the Association ID field is insufficient to identify the association uniquely within the scope of the source; when included, it must be set to a value that, together with the other fields in the object, identifies the association uniquely.
sections.plainLanguage: The original object gives a node only 65536 association numbers, and has no way to name an association that belongs to a whole operator rather than one node. The Extended objects add a global source field holding the operator's identifier and a variable-length field for extra identifying data. Everything else about how the object is matched and forwarded stays the same.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content:
Per RFC 4872, the ASSOCIATION object uses an object class number of the form 11bbbbbb so that nodes which do not support it remain compatible. Per RFC 2205, such nodes ignore the object but forward it without modification. That is also what happens for unknown association types.

Per RFC 4872, transit nodes that support the ASSOCIATION object but not the Extended Association C-Types transmit, without modification, any received ASSOCIATION object in the corresponding outgoing Path message. Per RFC 2205, an egress node that supports the ASSOCIATION object but not the Extended Association C-Types may generate an Unknown object C-Type error, and that error propagates to the ingress node for standard error processing.

The RFC advises that operators wishing to use a function supported by a particular association type should ensure that the type is supported on any node expected to act on the association.
sections.plainLanguage: Older nodes ignore an object they do not understand and pass it along untouched, so a mixed network keeps working. One gap remains: a node that does not know the Extended forms may report an error at the far end of the path, so operators should check that every node in the path supports the association type they intend to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the part of the document reviewing procedures from RFC 4872 and RFC 4873 defines no new procedures, and so introduces no new security considerations. Section 3 defines broader usage of the ASSOCIATION object but does not fundamentally expand on the association function. Section 4 increases the number of bits carried in an ASSOCIATION object by 32 and likewise does not expand on the association function. The broader definition does allow more information to be conveyed, but that information is not fundamentally different from what RSVP already carries, so no new risks are introduced.

For a general discussion of MPLS- and GMPLS-related security issues, including RSVP's chain of trust security model, the reader is pointed to the MPLS/GMPLS security framework in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security guidance of its own. It says the wider use of the object and the extra 32 bits do not create new risks, and points to RFC 5920 for how MPLS and GMPLS networks are secured in general.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned two new C-Types for the existing ASSOCIATION object, class number 199, in the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Parameters registry. C-Type 3 is the Type 3 IPv4 Extended Association and C-Type 4 is the Type 4 IPv6 Extended Association.

The document also broadens the potential usage of the Resource Sharing Association Type defined in RFC 4873, so the reference for that type in the associated registry was updated. The registry entry previously read 2 Resource Sharing (R) [RFC4873] and now reads 2 Resource Sharing (S) [RFC4873][RFC6780], which also corrects a duplicated use of the letter R.

No other IANA considerations are introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new object types are registered for the Extended ASSOCIATION objects, and the entry for the Resource Sharing association type is corrected. Nothing else changes in the registries.
